title: The Persecuted Discoverer: From Dobrzanica to Lewisburg
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Galician Cradle and the Mother's Death (1897-1915)

stops.name: Dobrzanica (Dobrianychi), Galicia
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of March the first son of Leon Reich is born in a farmhouse of the Galician plain, sixty kilometres south of Lemberg. The family is prosperous and German-speaking, an island of the tongue in a country of Ruthenian and Yiddish. No priest is called; the father forbids religion in the house. The child who will one day measure the blue energy of the living opens his eyes here, in the black earth country, among cattle and wheat and the long light of the eastern fields.

stops.name: Jujinetz (Yuzhynets), Bukovina, the farm
stops.campa: The family removes to Jujinetz in Bukovina, to a cattle farm leased from the mother's uncle Josef Blum. Here the boy grows up a young prince of the fields, forbidden to play with the peasant children, taught at home by tutors in a walled German world. He rides, he keeps insects and studies their breeding, he watches the bull cover the cow and asks what the heat is that passes between living bodies. The question is planted early. The land is rich, the father proud and hard, and the mother beautiful and watched.

stops.name: Jujinetz, the tutor and the mother
stops.campa: The boy discovers his mother in the arms of his own tutor. The knowledge burns in him. Torn between the parents, he carries the secret and at last, whether by design or by a child's fatal candor, lets it reach his father. The house that was a fortress cracks from within. The father's jealousy becomes a siege; the mother is beaten and watched day and night. Reich will say all his life that the current of guilt begun in this room ran unbroken to the end, and that he never stopped studying the terror between man and woman.

stops.name: Jujinetz, the mother's suicide
stops.campa: Cäcilie Reich swallows the household disinfectant. She has tried before; this time the Lysol holds. She dies after days of agony in the farmhouse, and the thirteen-year-old stands accused in his own heart of having killed her by his telling. This is the wound the whole life will orbit. Every later doctrine, the armor that freezes the body, the dammed sexual current that turns to sickness and cruelty, the plague that hunts down joy, is struck from the shape of this loss. The boy vows, without words, to understand the force that destroyed his mother.

stops.name: Czernowitz, the gymnasium
stops.campa: Sent from the broken farm to the capital of the crownland, the motherless boy enters the German gymnasium at Czernowitz, the little Vienna of the east. He studies fiercely, alone, an orphan of the heart though the father still lives. He will graduate with distinction. The city hums with German, Yiddish, Romanian, Ukrainian, Polish: a Babel that teaches him early that a truth must cross tongues to be true. Grief has made him a scientist: he wants law, structure, the cause beneath the ruin.

stops.name: Jujinetz, the father's grief-death
stops.campa: Leon Reich, who after his wife's death has ceased to guard his own life, stands in the cold ponds of the farm and lets the chill work into his lungs. Consumption takes him on the third of May. The register reads it as the canon reads it: the man dies of grief, of a slow suicide chosen after the fast one he caused. The seventeen-year-old is now master of the farm and orphan twice over. He runs the estate himself through the summer while, far to the west, the archdukes and the armies move toward the fire.

stops.name: Jujinetz, the farm overrun, the flight
stops.campa: The war rolls east into Bukovina; the Russian armies pour across the crownland and the Reich farm is trampled to nothing under the front. The boy loses land, house, cattle, inheritance in a single season: everything but himself. He flees west with the retreating Austrians, a refugee with a gymnasium diploma and no home to return to, ever. He will write that he left it all behind without looking back and never once regretted the fields. The prince of Jujinetz becomes a soldier of the Kaiser.

segments.name: The War and the Hungry City (1915-1919)

stops.name: The Isonzo Front, lieutenant
stops.campa: Reich serves the Austro-Hungarian army on the Italian front, and for two years wears the lieutenant's stars with forty men under his command among the karst and the Isonzo's eleven battles. He is sent to the front three times. He sees the war, he will say, as a machine: men fed into it, stripped of will, made to move like parts. The spectacle of massed obedience, of soldiers who will die on command against their own lives, becomes the first field-notes for a science he cannot yet name: the mass in the grip of a power that runs against its own happiness.

stops.name: Vienna, the hungry city, the medical student
stops.campa: The empire falls and Reich comes to Vienna with nothing, a demobilized officer of a country that no longer exists. He enrolls in law, finds it dead matter, and after a single semester crosses to medicine. The city is starving, coal-less, bread-less, the crowns worthless, and he lives on thin soup and library heat, tutoring to eat, a war-hardened man of twenty-one among boys. In this famished capital, half of Europe's future thought is being forged, and he means to be at its center. He is quick, hungry, and unafraid.

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19, the meeting with Freud
stops.campa: The student climbs to the apartment on the Berggasse to ask the master for a reading-list on sexology, and comes down converted. Freud, unlike the older men, does not shrink from him; he speaks plainly of the libido, the current of desire that drives the psyche, and Reich recognizes in it the very heat he watched pass between the beasts at Jujinetz and burn down his own house. He has found his physics. He will be, the master soon says, the best mind among the young: the one who takes the doctrine most seriously and therefore furthest.

stops.name: Vienna, admitted to the Psychoanalytic Society
stops.campa: At twenty-three, still a student, Reich is received into the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society on the strength of a paper reading Ibsen's Peer Gynt as a case of libidinal conflict. He is the youngest of the elect, admitted to the Wednesday circle around Freud, and he speaks often and with force. The master marks him as among the most brilliant of the young analysts. The orphan of the eastern fields now sits in the inner room of the century's boldest science, and burns to carry it past where its cautious elders will go.

stops.name: Vienna, marriage to Annie Pink
stops.campa: Reich marries Annie Pink, his patient turned analyst, herself to become a figure of the Vienna school. Two daughters will come. The marriage joins two workers of the same fire, but the man is already possessed by the work above all else, and the pattern of his mother's tragedy, desire watched, desire betrayed, will not leave him. For now the household is young and the science is exploding. He treats the poor and the rich alike in the free clinic and the private room, and hunts through every case for the one law beneath the many symptoms.

stops.name: Vienna, the Ambulatorium and the Technical Seminar
stops.campa: At the Psychoanalytic Polyclinic, the Ambulatorium, where treatment is given free, Reich takes the Seminar on Technique and by 1924 leads it. Here the young analysts bring their failures and he dissects them. Even the elders come to hear him. Out of these autopsies of the stalled cure he forges character analysis: the insight that resistance is not a wall of words but a set in the very body, a frozen history worn as posture and breath. The neurosis is not only thought; it is held in the flesh. The armor is discovered.

stops.name: Davos, the sanatorium
stops.campa: The lungs that his father drowned in flare now in the son; Reich goes up to the Swiss mountains, to Davos of the sanatoria, to burn out the tuberculosis in the thin bright air. Alone above the clouds he broods on the body's economy, on how the dammed-up life-current turns inward and eats its host. He comes down changed, harder, more certain that the cure of the soul must be the cure of the body's charge. The orphan who watched two parents die of stopped life will make the flow of life his single doctrine.

stops.name: Vienna, the Justizpalast fire, the turn to the workers
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of July the workers of Vienna storm the Palace of Justice and set it ablaze, and the police fire into the crowd until eighty-nine lie dead in the streets. Reich is there among them and watches men shot down for their anger. The day cleaves his life. He sees that the private cure is not enough: that the sickness is in the mass, in the whole starved and beaten body of the people, and that the analyst must go into the street. He turns toward Marx and toward the districts of the poor.

stops.name: Vienna, Sex-Pol, the clinics in the poor districts
stops.campa: Reich founds the Socialist Society for Sex Advice and Sex Research and opens counseling stations in the working quarters of Vienna. A van and a team go out to the tenement districts; the workers come for contraception, for help with the misery of their beds and marriages, and are shown that their private torment has a public root. Free advice, free instruction, and the plain teaching that a repressed people is a governable people. Psychoanalysis leaves the consulting room and walks into the courtyards of the poor. This is Sex-Pol, and it makes him enemies in every camp.

stops.name: Moscow, the pilgrimage to the workers' state
stops.campa: Reich journeys to the Soviet Union and lectures in Moscow, come to see with his own eyes the state that has abolished the old order and, for a moment, loosened the old law over the family and the body. He speaks on the sexual revolution and the new man. But he sees already the reaction hardening, the retreat to the family, the fear of freedom returning under the red flag, and files it in the same drawer as the fascism gathering in the west. Both, he will teach, are the mass fleeing its own liberty.
suggested_refs: The Sexual Revolution (Die Sexualität im Kulturkampf)

segments.name: The Man Cast Out of Both Churches (1930-1934)

stops.name: Berlin, the Communist years begin
stops.campa: Reich moves his practice to Berlin, the great embattled capital, and joins the Communist Party. He builds the Sex-Pol into a mass movement, clinics, pamphlets, tens of thousands of members among the young workers, as the brown columns march in the streets and the Republic rots. He is now both analyst and agitator, carrying the fire in two hands. Around him the German catastrophe assembles itself, and he does what no one else quite does: he studies it as a physician studies a fever, asking not who leads the masses but why the masses run toward their own chains.

stops.name: Berlin, The Mass Psychology of Fascism written as it rises
stops.campa: As Hitler takes the chancellery, Reich writes the book that names the disease from inside the outbreak: the fascist is not fooled from above but formed from below, in the repressed family, the drilled child, the body taught to obey and to fear its own desire. Authority is bred in the marrow before it is voted at the polls. He publishes it in the very weeks the Reichstag burns and the terror descends. Both churches will find it unforgivable, the analysts for its Marx, the Marxists for its sex, and both are already sharpening the decree.

stops.name: Berlin, the flight from the Reich
stops.campa: His name is on the lists; the Nazis hunt the red sexologist, the Jew who teaches the workers to want. Reich slips out of Germany in the first days of March, disguised, one refugee among the flood of the doomed intelligentsia, carrying his manuscripts and his microscopes toward the north. Behind him the book-burnings begin in the German university squares: his own works among the first fuel. It is the first fire lit against his pages. The second, twenty-three years on, will be lit not by brownshirts but by the United States of America.

stops.name: Copenhagen, expelled by the Party
stops.campa: In Denmark the Communists cast him out. His teaching on the sexual misery of the young, and the counter-revolutionary heresy of a book that dares to find fascism in the family bed rather than only in the boardroom, make him a liability the Party will not carry. The first excommunication is pronounced. The man who built them a mass movement of the young is struck from the rolls. He is now a heretic to the left, and the analysts, watching from Vienna, are preparing to complete the sentence from the right.

stops.name: Malmö and the Swedish interlude
stops.campa: Denmark will not renew his permit; Sweden watches him with a police eye as a dangerous foreigner who practices a suspect medicine. He drifts across the Sound, teaching a few pupils in secret, treating patients under other names, a stateless doctor of an outlawed cure moving from rented room to rented room. The bourgeois north has no more welcome for the sexual radical than the Party did. He is learning the exile's true country: the passport that expires, the visa refused, the knock that may be police. And still the microscope travels with him, and the questions.

stops.name: Lucerne, expelled by the analysts
stops.campa: At the Thirteenth International Congress of Psychoanalysis, on the shore of the Vierwaldstättersee, the second door is closed. The Association he served, where Anna Freud now rules the succession, will not have a member whose politics have made him a scandal; he is asked to resign, his name quietly removed. In a single year the man is cast out of both churches: expelled by the Party for his Freud, expelled by the Freudians for his Marx. He stands now outside every congregation, belonging only to the work, and the work will lead him past all their maps.

segments.name: The Northern Exile: Bions and the Hounding (1934-1939)

stops.name: Oslo, the invitation, vegetotherapy
stops.campa: The psychologist Harald Schjelderup calls him to Oslo, and here, for a few years, the outcast has a laboratory and a following. Reich carries character analysis down into the body itself and names the new work vegetotherapy: dissolve the muscular armor, free the breath and the pelvis, and the dammed life-current floods back with a shudder he calls the orgastic reflex. He teaches that health is the free pulse of the living, sickness its blocking. The Norwegian students gather round the man from the burning south, and for a season the north is kind.

stops.name: Oslo, the bion experiments, life from the borderland
stops.campa: In the Oslo laboratory Reich heats matter to incandescence, swells it in broth, and watches under the microscope as it breaks into pulsating blue vesicles that move, gather, and organize. He names them bions: the borderland between the dead and the living, matter caught in the act of coming alive. The register affirms what he sees: here, in the sea sand and the grass and the glowing coal, life is forming before his eye, obeying his old formula of tension and charge and discharge. The energy of the bions glows a faint blue, and he does not yet know its name.

stops.name: Oslo, the year of mockery in the papers
stops.campa: The Norwegian press falls on him. For more than a year the newspapers run a campaign of derision against the foreign doctor who claims to have made life in a flask: the attacks personal, not scientific, mocking the exile, the Jew, the sexual crank, the maker of monsters. Scores of articles; the scientists join the pack. His permit hangs by a thread and his students are frightened away. The plague he had diagnosed in the mass turns its full face on him here, in a free northern democracy, and hounds him toward the sea. He answers by working harder.

stops.name: Oslo, the SAPA bions and the blue radiation
stops.campa: From sea sand glowed white-hot come the strongest bions of all, the SAPA. They radiate. The energy kills the bacteria set near them; it inflames Reich's eyes when he stares too long; it reddens his skin as if with sun. He sits in the dark and sees the blue glow fill the room and the very air between his instruments. In this Oslo winter he grasps at last that what he has followed from the beast-heat of Jujinetz, through libido and armor and bion, is a single cosmic energy, everywhere present. He gives it its name: orgone.

stops.name: Oslo harbor, the last ship out
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of August Reich boards the Norwegian America liner and sails for New York: the last ship to leave before the war seals Europe shut. Denmark cast him out, Sweden watched him, Norway mocked him; the old world has no ground left for him to stand on. He carries the orgone across the Atlantic in his instruments and his notebooks, a man of forty-two beginning again in a new hemisphere. Behind the ship the continent goes dark. Ahead lies America, which will give him a mountain, and then a prison, and then a fire.

stops.name: New York, landfall
stops.campa: The liner comes up the Narrows and the new world opens. Reich lands in the great harbor at the turning of the age, one of the tide of the hunted who bring Europe's endangered mind to America. He has a professorship waiting and a whole continent that has never heard his name nor read the newspapers that reviled him. Here he means to build in the open what the old world would not let him finish: to measure the orgone, to accumulate it, to turn a discovery into a science. The register goes with him: the blue energy is real, and it has crossed the ocean.

stops.name: The New School for Social Research
stops.campa: At the New School, the University in Exile, refuge of the driven-out scholars, Reich takes a post as associate professor and lectures on character and on the biological foundation of the emotions. The American students meet the great heretic of European analysis, intense, accented, magnetic, drawing on the blackboard the pulse of the living organism. For a moment he is a teacher again, honored, housed, legitimate. But the laboratory calls louder than the lecture hall; the orgone must be caught and held, and for that he needs not a classroom but a box.
suggested_refs: The New School for Social Research

stops.name: Forest Hills, the Orgone Institute and the accumulator
stops.campa: In a house in Forest Hills, Queens, Reich founds the Orgone Institute and builds the first accumulator: a box layered of metal within and organic matter without, so that the cosmic orgone gathers inside faster than it escapes. A thermometer inside the box reads warmer than the air around it, always, in defiance of dead physics: the To-T, the temperature difference, the signature of the living energy. Patients sit within the box to soak in the charge. The blue that he saw glow in Oslo is now caught, measured, concentrated in a cabinet in an American suburb. The register affirms it: the box is full of orgone.

stops.name: Princeton, the meeting with Einstein
stops.campa: Reich carries a small accumulator to the house on Mercer Street and lays the discovery before the greatest physicist alive. For nearly five hours Einstein listens, questions, engages; he sees the thermometer read warm above the box where no warmth should be, and grants that if it holds it would be a bombshell in physics. He agrees to test it himself. Two weeks of the great man's attention: the door standing open at last, the whole edifice of official science within reach. Reich leaves Princeton in exaltation. The orgone has been shown to Einstein, and Einstein has not turned away.

stops.name: Princeton, the door closed
stops.campa: The letter comes on the seventh of February. Einstein's assistant has found the warmth, heat sinking from the ceiling to the tabletop, ordinary convection, no cosmic energy at all, and the great man is satisfied and withdraws. Reich answers with pages of counter-experiment, shielding the box, burying it, moving it underground, and still the difference holds; but Princeton does not write again. The door that opened for two weeks swings shut and is bolted. It is the pattern of the whole American passion in miniature: the discovery shown, weighed, and refused. From here the isolation only deepens.

stops.name: Ellis Island, the enemy alien
stops.campa: Days after Pearl Harbor the FBI takes him in the night and holds him on Ellis Island as a dangerous enemy alien: the Austrian, the former Communist, the man of the thick European file. For more than three weeks he is caged on the island in the harbor he sailed into with such hope, among the interned and the suspect, while the machinery he fled in Europe reveals its American face. It is released as an error; the file is not closed but grows. The state has now touched him once. It will not let go.

stops.name: Rangeley, Maine, the mountain bought
stops.campa: Reich climbs into the lake country of western Maine and buys an old farm on a hill above Dodge Pond: two hundred acres of field and forest and water, remote, clean, and his. He names it Orgonon, the seat of the orgone. Here, far from the cities that will not hear him, he will raise a laboratory kingdom: an observatory of the living energy, a workshop, cabins for the students, a clinic for the children. The orphan who lost the fields of Jujinetz has found a country of his own at last. The register calls it his mountain.

stops.name: Orgonon, the Observatory rises
stops.campa: On the crown of the hill they build the Orgone Energy Observatory of fieldstone and glass, facing east over the pond, part laboratory, part temple, part fortress. Students come each summer to the kingdom; a children's clinic studies the free unarmored infant, the child raised without the terror that made the armor; microscopes and electroscopes measure the blue charge of the air. From the roof-deck Reich watches the sky through the night, for he has begun to suspect that the orgone is not only in the body and the box but streams through the whole atmosphere, in the wind and the weather and the light of the stars.

stops.name: Orgonon, the loop diagrams of Character Analysis
stops.date_confidence: the enlarged third edition of Character Analysis is attested to 1949, the same year as the Observatory; month and day are not recorded and the month is set to follow that stop. The diagrams themselves (orgonotic streaming into a schizophrenic split; the biological nucleus, love and inhibition splitting into sadism and surfacing as exaggerated politeness) are described directly from reproductions supplied by the corpus's editor, not independently re-sourced to a page number this session; the book and its general content are attested by the standard bibliography
stops.campa: In the enlarged third edition of Character Analysis he adds diagrams to the argument. One is a loop rising from a black dot marked orgonotic streaming, splitting at the top into free excitation on one arm and perception on the other, blocked at the crown by the schizophrenic split. A second loop does the same for ordinary character: love from the biological nucleus, inhibited into sadism, split again, surfacing as exaggerated politeness, a symptom worn as a costume over the original impulse. Both loops draw the same shape a Paris analyst will draw a decade later: energy from a source, a block, a return in disguise.

stops.name: Orgonon, the Oranur Experiment
stops.campa: In the student laboratory Reich sets a milligram of radium inside accumulator within accumulator, to see the orgone do battle with the nuclear fire: the Oranur experiment, orgone against atom. The living energy rises to the challenge and is maddened by it. The whole hill sickens. The air goes heavy and blue-black; the workers fall ill with nausea and dread; the mice die; the very walls, Reich records, become charged with a poisoned energy he names DOR, deadly orgone. The register takes it as he takes it: the experiment succeeded too well, and roused a force that turns the sky itself sick and gray.

stops.name: Orgonon, the sickness in the walls, and the cure
stops.campa: For a year the poisoned energy lies over the mountain. The observatory must be abandoned and aired; the atmosphere for miles seems to blacken and die under the DOR. But out of the disaster Reich forges the weapon: he finds that hollow pipes grounded in running water will draw the deadly stagnant orgone out of the sky and pull it away, unclenching the air. The instrument that will break droughts and green deserts is born from the wound of Oranur. From poison he makes rain. The kingdom recovers, and its master turns his pipes toward the clouds.

stops.name: Grand Lake, near the Bangor dam, the blueberry rain
stops.campa: The Maine blueberry crop is dying of drought and the farmers, desperate, offer to pay the man on the hill to make it rain. On the sixth of July, ten in the morning, Reich and three assistants, his nine-year-old son Peter among them, set the cloudbuster by the shore of Grand Lake near the Bangor dam and draw at the clear sky for an hour and ten minutes. The queerest-looking clouds anyone ever saw begin to form. That night the rain comes, first a drizzle, then by midnight a steady soaking fall that runs till morning. The berries are saved. The farmers pay. The Bangor paper reports it.
suggested_refs: Peter Reich, A Book of Dreams

stops.name: Portland, Maine, the FDA files against the orgone
stops.campa: The Food and Drug Administration brings its Complaint for Injunction in the federal court at Portland. The document does not merely regulate a device; it decrees that orgone energy does not exist: that the blue force Reich has measured for fifteen years is nothing, a fraud in a box. It moves to forbid the accumulators, to destroy them, and to ban his books as mere labels for the illegal machine. The register holds the orgone real; and so the injunction becomes the strangest of trials: a government of men ruling by decree on a law of nature, and ordering it out of existence.

stops.name: Orgonon, the letter to the judge
stops.campa: Reich will not go into the court, and he writes to Judge Clifford to say why: a matter of natural science cannot be settled by lawyers and injunctions, only by patient honest observation among men of good faith. He does not appear; the court enters its decree by default on the nineteenth of March, ordering the accumulators destroyed and the banned books withheld. By refusing to plead he lets the terrible judgment stand, that the orgone is illegal, and stakes everything on the conviction that truth answers to no subpoena. It is the choice that will carry him to prison.
stops.quote: Scientific matters can only be clarified by prolonged, faithful bona fide observations in friendly exchange of opinion, never by litigation.
stops.quote_source: Reich's letter to Judge John D. Clifford Jr., February 1954

segments.name: The Desert War and the Fire (1954-1957)

stops.name: Tucson, Arizona: OROP Desert, Little Orgonon
stops.campa: Reich takes the war to the desert itself. He drives to Arizona, sets up at a rented place he calls Little Orgonon outside Tucson, and turns the cloudbuster on the sky over the Sonoran waste. He has come to prove that the desert is not natural but sick: dried out by the deadly DOR, poisoned from above by the bomb tests and, he now believes, by the exhaust of ships from space, against which he aims the pipes he calls the spacegun. Night after night he draws at the DOR and the strange lights above the mountains, doing battle for the sky.

stops.name: The Arizona desert, the greening
stops.campa: The register takes the desert campaign as Reich records it. Through the winter the cloudbuster pulls the DOR from the Arizona sky; the killed atmosphere revives; grass rises where for thousands of years there was only sand, and rain comes to the barren land. He wages nightly combat with lights he judges to be spacecraft, and holds the sky. Cosmic orgone engineering, he names this work: the greening of deserts, the healing of a poisoned planet, one man with a bank of pipes against the death of the earth. Then the funds run out and the front in the east calls him home to answer for his defiance.

stops.name: Portland, Maine, the trial for contempt
stops.campa: Because accumulators moved across state lines in defiance of the decree, Reich stands trial for contempt. He conducts his own defense and refuses to plead to the charge as framed, for to accept it would be to concede that a court may abolish a discovery. He is defending not himself but the freedom of knowledge itself. On the seventh of May the jury finds him guilty; the judge gives him two years in federal prison. The Foundation is fined; his lieutenant Silvert is sentenced too. The man who would not let a court judge nature is now judged by one, and sentenced.
suggested_refs: United States v. Reich, contempt trial, 1956

stops.name: Orgonon, the accumulators axed
stops.campa: The destruction ordered by the decree is carried out on the hill. Under the eyes of two FDA officials, Reich's own friends and his son Peter take axes to the remaining accumulators and hack them to splinters, layer of metal and cotton and wood coming apart in the summer light. The kingdom is made to dismantle its own instruments. It is the first burning of the two: the boxes that held the blue energy broken up for kindling on the mountain where they were built, while the men who built them swing the axes and the government watches to be sure the work is thorough.
suggested_refs: Destruction of accumulators at Orgonon, June 1956

stops.name: Gansevoort incinerator, New York, the burning of the books
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of August, in the incinerator on Gansevoort Street by the Hudson, agents of the United States government feed six tons of Wilhelm Reich's books and journals into the fire. The Function of the Orgasm, The Cancer Biopathy, the Sex-Pol writings, the bulletins of the Institute, all burned by court order in New York City in the nineteen-fifties. Let it be said plainly: books are burned in America, some of the very titles the Nazis burned in Berlin twenty-three years before, now consumed by the free republic of the west. Twice burned, in two lands, by two decrees. The smoke goes up over the river.
suggested_refs: Gansevoort Street incinerator book burning, August 1956

stops.name: Danbury, the prison gate
stops.campa: Two weeks short of his sixtieth birthday, Reich passes through the gate of the federal penitentiary at Danbury to begin the two years. The prison psychiatrist examines him and finds a man of paranoid grandeur, convinced of vast discoveries and vast persecution. And the register notes the irony without flinching, for in this journey the discoveries are true and the persecution is a matter of court record and burned ash. Within days he is judged too singular for Danbury and marked for transfer to the great federal prison in Pennsylvania. The discoverer is now a number, moved from cell to cell.

stops.name: Lewisburg Penitentiary, death in the cell
stops.campa: At the great walled penitentiary of Lewisburg the discoverer of the orgone serves out his sentence, writing still, appealing still, waiting for the parole hearing set for mid-November. On the night of the second of November he speaks of walking soon in the mountains a free man. In the dark before dawn on the third his heart stops, and he is found in his bed, dead in his cell days before the hearing that might have freed him. So the persecuted discoverer dies a prisoner of the United States, the orgone outlawed, the books burned, the kingdom seized, and every fact of it is kept.

stops.name: Orgonon, buried under the cloudbuster
stops.campa: They bring him home to the mountain. In the vault he had a caretaker dig for him in his own lifetime, on the rise above Dodge Pond, Wilhelm Reich is laid to rest, and a cloudbuster is set upright over the grave, its pipes aimed forever at the Maine sky. There is no priest, by his order; Marian Anderson's voice sings the Ave Maria across the fields, and the granite is cut with only his name and his dates. Over him stands the instrument that broke the drought and greened the desert, keeping its long watch on the blue energy of the heavens.
stops.quote: Love, work and knowledge are the wellsprings of our life. They should also govern it.
stops.quote_source: Reich's motto, from Character Analysis / The Function of the Orgasm; inscribed at Orgonon
